questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to attend a university where English is the main language – preferably at a destination that I wouldn't otherwise visit on vacation.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The school system (grading, midterms, assignments, attendace) is quite dfferent from the Danish school system. It demands more continuous engagement, which drages the score a bit down. As a Molecular Biomedicine student, I was only used to attending 1-2 courses per. block. At McGill you would have to attend four different courses at once – each having more continuous school work to be done, compared to the structure in Denmark (or at least at Molecular Biomedicine).

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
I had some issues accessing my McGill mail before arrival at he University. I therefore missed some information fra the University that I should have reacted to – but it all worked out fine. I think McGill's portals are easier to navigate compared to UCPH. 
I think it would have been to know upon arrival, that McGill charges a (fairly high) mandetory cost of International Health Care – and that to avoid paying this as a Danish Student, you need to apply for extension before receiving RAMQ (that can't be applied for before arriving in Canada).

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: IT-support.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I didn't attend the introduction week. But the university is overall fairly helpfull.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: We talked with former exchange students that got us in contact with a landlord in the city, who had an apartment hat we could rent. I would not say that this is the case for any other exchange students I talked to. Most live in student accommodation or found roomies via FB groups or -marked place. My advice is therefore to consult former exchange-students to see if they have any contacts or use FB.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It really depends on where you live! We lived in Le Plateau which is both close to campus and a really nice neighborhood!
The apartment standard is not the same in Canada as it is in Copenhagen, but it'll work fine. Many of the international students, that are only there for one semester, often get student accommodation quite far from campus and it's quite expensive compared to what you get – and there's a mandetory meal plan. I (and the people who lived in student accommodation) would therefore recommend finding an apartment on you own!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I don't remember the process in great detail, but I remember that there where a lot of documents that I needed to obtain and send alongside my application. But there was a guide to do so, so it wasn't too hard. 
Registration for courses was on the other hand not a too positive experience to be honest. Upon registration I used their visual schedule builder that helped me choose courses that aligned with each other. What they don't tell you is that the McGill students (non exchange) gets to register before the exchange students do. One of the courses i wanted to attend was therefore fully before I could registere – sometimes if you write directly to the professor they can admit you in the course anyways. The schedule builder or website also don't show if you aren't able to take a course as an exchange student – which was the case for the course I wanted to attend the most. The course still has available seats but I wasn't allowed to registre even after consulting the course professor.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: A step-by-step guide was provided and schedule builder.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I had five courses that I wanted to attend – where I would drop the one i liked the least within the two week drop-periode. 
I 'only' got three out of the five, with one of the ones I didn't get being the course I wanted the most. I would therefore give it a 5/10.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Look into if you as an exchange student are able to attend a given course – or email the course professor before registration. 
Sometimes it will say that the course is only for a specific major, but that is not always the case. 
Also, have backups in case the course you want gets full!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Some of my courses focus on 'unnecessary' memorization instead of unterstanding concepts – which is very different from UCPH. 
Some courses have exams as multiple choice but here the focus is also on 'unnecessary' memorization and not concepts – which can be frustrating when knowing the course material but can remember the name of some small protein. 
There is also way more work to be done during the semester that counts towards your final grade – kinda like high school in Denmark. It can be a bit hard to find a balance with school work and social life/trips, but I made it work! The good thing about this model is that you can have passed your course before even attending the exam – as the exam often 'only' ranges from 20-50% of the final grade.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Some of my courses was entry level (level 200) while I also had 300- and 500-level courses. I don't think it necessarily is the level of the course that determines the difficulty. I had a 250 and 575 course that was equally challenging – and my least challenging courses. 
My 300-course was a entry to med-school course (which I didn't know upon regestration) which made it more difficult.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: For most of my courses there is only lectures and no to very little course literature. A three credit course has three hours of lectures per week – either as three one-hour lectures, two one-and-half-hour lectures or one three-hour lecture. By default they don't do breaks in the lectures – not even the three-hours ones which is very different from UCPH. The humanities courses often also have conferences which is a participation class-lecture as we know it from High School. Conferences often consists of 20-30 students and a TA where you get a grade for participation and sometimes also presentations.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
BIOL 575 – Human Biochemical Genetics 
ANAT 365 – Cellular Trafficking 
COMP 204 – Computer Programming for Life Sciences 
GSFS 250 – Sexual and Gender Diversity Studies

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Basically all of them but for different reasons. 
BIOL 575 is an 'easy' course as a Molecular Biomedicine student. More of the curriculum aligns with former courses and the topics are very relevant and interesting.
ANAT 365 was most definitely my hardest course that aquired a lot of attention – mostly due to the exam forms and research project. The curriculum was on the other hand very interesting. 
COMP 204 is nice if you want intro to python! It does take a lot of weakly work since there's both weekly assignments, quizzes and videos to watch. But you learn a lot! 
GSFS 250 is nice since it's non science so you get to do something completely different. Also the curriculum is very good and should be something every body knew!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries are more expensive in Canada! Eating out on the other hand is a bit cheaper than in Denmark – we therefore, and because it's cozy, ate out a lot:)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Basically everything! There's a activity's night in the beginning of the semester where you can meet all the different clubs. On the unis website you can also sign up for different types of sports.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I attended the Nordic Culture Club and the Knitting Club – both really nice! I was also a part of the McGill Choral Society which consists of people of all ages – also really nice! We did a huge church concert in the end of the semester. 
I know some of the others attended tennis-classes. There is free access to the uni pool and it's cheap to sign into the uni gym.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go to Banff!!!! It's a national park i Alberta that for me is a must visit if you're into nature and hiking. It's the most beautiful place I've been so far.  
We also went to NYC – the school arranges busses to different locations in the reading break, which I really recommend. 
Otherwise we went a trip to Vermont and on hiking day-trips in the 'local' area. If you're up for a longer trip, then Toronto is also a nice visit! Ideally you can drive up to Ottowa (The Capital of Canada) on the way:) 
It's fairly easy and cheap to rent a car – you can get student discounts through the university.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The culture is somewhat european but also very northern american. It really helps if you know some French (I didn't) but as long as you stay in the cities people speak English.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join the clubs! Also don't be afraid to talk to people in your classes! It's true that Canadians are (overly) friendly:)

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The amount of homeless people was for me the biggest cultural difference for me. 
That and the amount of French that are spoken on the street/in shops/cafés.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How friendly people are!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Be open to new things, go on trips and enjoy the canadian culture, and remember that money will come back but your exchange stay won't:)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Nope.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I made! A lot of them also being Danish, that I get to hang out with post-exchange as well! And the rest has promised to visit me in Copenhagen – and also gives me a good reason to return to the city in the future:)

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The amount of school-work! But I ended up doing more than just fine, so try not to stress too much about it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
